turns.response_html:
Based on the photo, these are LED tube lights, specifically designed as modern, energy-efficient replacements for traditional 4-foot fluorescent tubes.

From the packaging, we can identify several key details:

  • Style: These are Linear T8 LED tubes (they also fit T12 fixtures).
  • Brightness: 1825 lumens, which is standard for a bright workspace or garage.
  • Brand: This specific 10-pack with the yellow "Important Safety Warning" label is the Great Value (Walmart) brand.

What do they plug into?

These lights are designed to fit into 4-foot (48-inch) fluorescent ceiling fixtures with standard G13 medium bi-pin sockets (the two small metal prongs at each end).

However, how they "plug in" depends on your specific fixture:

  • Existing Ballasts: The warning label states these are designed to work with magnetic, electronic instant start, program start, and rapid start ballasts. This means you can often simply "plug and play"—remove your old fluorescent bulb and put this one in without any wiring changes.
  • Ballast Bypass (Type B): The label also hints at a "ballast bypass" option. If your fixture's ballast is old or broken, you (or an electrician) can rewire the fixture to send power directly to the sockets, bypassing the ballast entirely. This is often more reliable long-term.
  • Fixture Type: They are most commonly found in "shop lights" in garages, basements, laundry rooms, or commercial office troffers.

A Quick Tip for You

Since you're currently setting up your life in Ames and looking at apartments, if you're planning to use these in a rental, stick to the "plug and play" method. Just swap the bulbs so you can easily put the original ones back when you move out without having messed with the building's wiring!

turns.prompt_text: what kind of socket do they plug into
turns.response_html:
They plug into G13 medium bi-pin sockets, which are the standard two-prong connectors found at both ends of traditional 4-foot fluorescent fixtures.

Would you like me to find a photo of that specific socket to help you identify it in your fixture?

These sockets are often called "tombstones" because of their shape. To install the lights, you slide the two pins on the end of the tube into the center slot and then rotate the bulb 90 degrees to lock it into place and make the electrical connection.

You will find these in a variety of fixtures, such as:

  • Shop Lights: Often hung by chains in garages or basements.
  • Troffers: The recessed rectangular fixtures common in office ceilings.
  • Under-cabinet fixtures: Longer 4-foot versions used for workspace lighting.

Because you have an interest in DIY electronics and technical projects, you might find it useful to know that these sockets come in "shunted" and "non-shunted" versions. If you ever decide to bypass a ballast for a more permanent LED setup, checking which version your fixture has is a key step in the wiring process.

turns.prompt_text: what's the difference between shunted and non shunted
turns.response_html:
The main difference is how electrical current flows through the socket's internal contacts.

Shunted Sockets

  • Wiring: The two internal contacts are joined together (shorted).
  • Current: Power flows through a single path to both pins of the bulb.
  • Use Case: Common in Instant Start ballasts.
  • Visual: Usually has only one wire entry hole or terminal.

Non-Shunted Sockets

  • Wiring: The two internal contacts are kept separate.
  • Current: Power flows through two independent paths (one to each pin).
  • Use Case: Required for Rapid Start, Programmed Start, or specific LED ballast-bypass (Type B) wiring where the bulb needs a neutral and hot wire on the same end.
  • Visual: Usually has two or more wire entry holes or terminals.

Would you like me to find a guide on how to use a multimeter to test which type you have?

A ballast is a component that regulates the electrical current sent to a light bulb. Because fluorescent and some LED tubes cannot manage their own power intake, the ballast provides an initial high-voltage "kick" to start the lamp and then limits the current to prevent the bulb from overheating or exploding.

Why it matters for your LEDs:

  • Plug-and-Play (Type A): Uses the existing ballast already in your ceiling.
  • Ballast Bypass (Type B): Requires you to remove the ballast and wire the sockets directly to your building's power.

If you hear a buzzing sound or see flickering in your old fixtures, that's usually a sign the ballast is failing.
